episode.observableAction: Late on a cool Saturday morning, the subject and younger sibling play with a small red plastic ball in the shared courtyard, rolling it back and forth between the laundry lines and a low wall. After a harder roll, the ball glances off a bicycle stand and disappears under a row of stacked wooden pallets near the rubbish bins. The subject and sibling walk over, crouch down and peer into the narrow gap, but they cannot see the ball clearly in the shadows. The sibling reaches an arm in, brushes dust and a bottle cap, and pulls back empty-handed. The subject lies on their side on the concrete, stretches an arm under the pallets, and feels around, then withdraws with only grit on their fingers. Hearing their raised voices, the caregiver comes down the stairs carrying a laundry basket, sets it on a nearby bench, and asks where the ball went. The subject points under the pallets. The caregiver kneels, tries to tilt the top pallet, finds it too heavy to move alone, and instead suggests checking the other side. The subject and sibling circle around the stack, scanning the ground and poking with a short broken broom handle the caregiver has picked up from beside the bins. The subject pushes the handle into the gap from one side while the caregiver shines a small keyring torch from the other, guiding the subject to move the stick slightly left and right. After a few attempts, the ball rolls out from under the pallets toward the sibling’s shoes. The sibling grabs it, brushes off the dust on their trousers, and the three of them carry the broom handle and laundry basket back toward the stairs, with the subject and sibling resuming their rolling game a few metres away from the pallets.

episode.observableAction: On a mild afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject kneels beside a low wall, patting the ground and checking under a plastic chair, saying they cannot find their small red toy car. At the subject’s request, the caregiver sets the basket down and joins the search, lifting a corner of a faded outdoor rug, looking behind a bucket, and asking where the car was last seen. The subject and sibling look under a bicycle and along a crack by the drain while the caregiver checks the steps by the building door. On a breezy late afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject and younger sibling stand near the drying lines with a single slightly flat football. The subject reaches out, takes the ball from the sibling’s hands, and places it on the ground again, nudging it with their foot toward the chalk mark. The sibling frowns, grabs the ball as it rolls, and hugs it to their chest, saying it is their turn to choose. For a short moment they both hold onto the ball, each pulling in a different direction. The subject then lets go, walks a few steps away, and says they will only play if they can kick at the wall. The sibling stands still with the ball, looks at the chalk mark, and after a pause walks over and sets the ball on the ground in front of it. The subject comes back, taps the ball with their foot toward the mark, and the sibling follows behind, now joining in by taking the next kick.

The drawing shows a boxy tram with four uneven wheels and a row of square windows, with a thick dark line above it that the subject is slowly shading in. Other children talk quietly at nearby tables while a teacher moves between groups. The subject leans over the page, presses a green pencil hard along the top line, and then switches to a grey pencil to darken a short section. A few minutes later, the bell rings and the class is dismissed. The subject carefully slides the drawing into their school folder and walks out with the others. 

Later that day, in the shared courtyard of the home building, the grandparent sits on a low stool near the drying lines, folding dry shirts into a plastic basket. The subject comes through the building door carrying their school bag, sets it down by the wall, and pulls out the folder. They take out the tram drawing and hold it up at chest height. The grandparent glances over, pauses their folding, and asks what the picture is. The subject steps closer and turns the page so it faces the grandparent. The grandparent wipes their hands on their trousers, leans forward, and looks at the page, pointing with one finger at the dark line above the tram. They ask if that part is the wire the tram hangs from. The subject nods and traces the same line with a fingertip, then taps one of the square windows. The grandparent comments that the tram looks like the one at the loop, mentioning the bend where they sometimes wait together. The subject adds a quick pencil mark at the front of the tram, then lowers the page and slides it back into the folder while the grandparent returns to folding clothes.

After a short pause, the subject walks over, watches the pretend fishing, and suggests that after the sibling catches three fish, the hanger can become a steering wheel so they can drive the fish to a market. The sibling looks up, considers this, and nods, agreeing to count each pretend fish out loud while the subject waits beside them.

The grandparent steps back beside a pillar, watching while the subject studies the chart, counts coins into their palm, and moves to an unoccupied machine. The subject selects the route on the screen, hesitates, glances back once, and the grandparent simply nods without approaching. The subject inserts the coins, presses the button for a child ticket, and waits as the machine whirs and prints. When the ticket and a few coins drop into the tray, the subject picks them up, checks the printed stop name against the sign, and walks back to the grandparent, who takes the change but leaves the ticket in the subject’s hand as they move toward the waiting tram doors with other passengers.

In an overcast early afternoon science lesson, the class gathers around lab benches as the teacher floats a metal paperclip on water in a plastic tray, adds a drop of dish soap so it sinks, then invites students to try; the subject repeats the setup at a side tray, first touching the water with a fingertip that has only a trace of soap so the paperclip merely wobbles, then, after calling the teacher over and hearing that there may not have been enough soap, adds a full visible drop and watches the paperclip immediately sink.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: surface tension of water affected by soap

episodes.observableAction: On a cool late afternoon at the tram terminus, the grandparent and the subject step off a tram and walk together toward the row of small shops beside the loop. Near a corner grocery, the grandparent stops, takes a folded shopping list and some notes and coins from a pocket, and hands them to the subject while pointing at the shop door and saying they will wait on a nearby bench. The grandparent sits down facing the entrance as the subject goes inside alone, joins a short queue, checks the list, and picks up a loaf of bread and a carton of milk from low shelves. At the counter, the subject places the items down, waits while the shopkeeper rings them up, then counts out the notes and coins, hesitates briefly, and adds one more coin when the total is repeated. After receiving a small handful of change and a printed receipt, the subject tucks them into a pocket, carries the bag back outside, and walks straight to the bench, where the grandparent glances into the bag, nods once, and stands up so they can return together toward the tram platforms.

On a dim late afternoon at the tram terminus, the subject steps off a tram alone and walks straight to the row of small shops beside the loop, taking a folded note from their pocket and glancing once toward the benches where the grandparent usually waits, finding them empty. The subject pauses, then continues into the same corner grocery they have visited before, picks up a basket, and moves along the aisles, checking the note and selecting a loaf of bread, a carton of milk, and a small bag of rice from the shelves without speaking to anyone. At the counter, the subject places the items down, waits while the shopkeeper rings them up, and pulls a mix of notes and coins from their pocket, counting out the total the shopkeeper states without asking for confirmation. When the shopkeeper hands over a few coins of change and a receipt, the subject nods, tucks both into a pocket, and carries the bag back out to the tram loop, where they walk directly toward the platform entrance and join a short line of passengers waiting to board the next tram home.

At the neighborhood community workshop lending shelf, the subject helps a younger neighbor choose between a sports magazine and a bicycle repair booklet by showing pages and diagrams, then they both sign the borrowing sheet for the chosen booklet and leave together.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: introductory bicycle repair booklet from community workshop lending shelf

episodes.observableAction: At the community workshop lending shelf, the subject and a younger neighbor compare a comic-style bicycle tricks booklet and a thicker "Basic Bike Maintenance" booklet, the subject highlighting repair diagrams and a flyer for a Saturday repair session until the neighbor returns the tricks booklet, takes the maintenance one, and accompanies the subject to sign it out before they leave together for the street.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Basic Bike Maintenance" community workshop booklet

episodes.observableAction: On an early Saturday evening in the community workshop hall, folding chairs face a low platform where a local poet reads short pieces into a microphone as the subject and younger neighbor sit side by side near the middle with programs on their laps, having followed a handwritten flyer from the lending shelf; during a poem that quickly mixes English and Arabic, some adults in the back shift in their seats and an older man near the door mutters that he cannot follow it, the neighbor whispers that poems should stay in one language so people can understand and taps the English-only title on the program, and when the poem ends the subject claps steadily while the neighbor claps briefly, folds their arms, and keeps watching as the poet introduces the next piece.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: bilingual live poetry performance at community workshop

sliceECharacterization.note: Characterization only: developmental richness and intellectual formation are measured, never required as an admission gate.

episode.observableAction: On a dry afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject and the younger sibling use a half-deflated rubber ball to play a throwing game against the wall near the laundry lines. The subject stands several paving stones away from the wall and announces, “You have to stand back here and if you miss you’re out.” The sibling walks closer to the wall, toes almost touching it, and tosses the ball gently so it taps the bricks and rolls back. The subject shakes their head, steps over, and drags the sibling by the elbow back to the earlier paving stone, saying, “No, from here, that’s the rule.” The sibling pulls their arm away, steps forward again, and says, “I’m little, I go closer.” The ball rolls toward the drain while they talk. The subject picks it up, plants a foot on the paving stone line, and says, “Okay, you can be one step closer but you have to throw harder.” They place the ball in the sibling’s hands and point to a spot one tile nearer the wall. The sibling nods, moves to the indicated tile, and throws the ball harder this time. After it bounces back between them, they continue taking turns from their agreed spots, counting how many throws they can make without missing the wall.

modelOutput.observableAction: On a dry afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject and younger sibling play a throwing game with a half-deflated rubber ball against the wall near the laundry lines, briefly argue about how far from the wall the sibling must stand, adjust the rule so the sibling can stand one step closer if throwing harder, and then continue taking turns from their agreed spots, counting how many throws they make without missing the wall.

episode.observableAction: On a cool mid-morning in the shared courtyard, the subject sits on the concrete near the laundry lines using a small plastic bucket as a goal for rolling a scuffed tennis ball, counting softly each time the ball drops in. The younger sibling comes out carrying a toy car, takes the bucket without asking, and begins driving the car up and down its rim, making engine noises. The subject reaches for the bucket and says they still need it for the ball game, while the sibling pulls it closer and insists they are using it as a garage. After a brief back-and-forth over whose turn it is with the bucket, the subject picks up the ball and stands waiting, and the sibling finally slides the empty bucket back across the ground, saying they will use the car on the step instead. The subject sets the bucket back in place and resumes rolling the ball into it while the sibling moves a short distance away to play with the car on the courtyard step.

On a breezy afternoon at the neighborhood community workshop, the subject walks in beside their caregiver during an open-house event where local groups have set up tables. Near the front, a volunteer has taped several hand-painted posters to a folding display board, including one showing a tram crossing the river at sunset. The subject stops in front of that poster, steps closer until they are almost touching the board, and leans their head to one side while looking at the thick orange and purple brushstrokes in the sky. The caregiver pauses a few steps ahead, notices the subject has stopped, and comes back to stand next to them. The subject lifts a hand toward the poster without touching it, tracing the air along the uneven line of the bridge, then shifts their gaze to the way the paint has been dabbed into small dots to make the tram windows. After a few moments, the caregiver reads the small handwritten label under the picture aloud, and the subject nods once, keeps looking at the painted tram, and then finally turns away when another family squeezes in to see the same board.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: hand-painted poster of a tram crossing the river at sunset

episode.observableAction: In the practical science room at school on a winter afternoon, the class gathers around a lab bench while the teacher fills a clear glass with tap water and slowly slides a stiff piece of white card over the top. Holding the card in place with one hand, the teacher flips the glass upside down over a tray and then carefully removes the supporting hand so the card stays pressed against the mouth of the glass and the water does not spill. Several students murmur, and the teacher explains that the air underneath is pushing up on the card. When the teacher sets the glass back upright and tips the water into the tray, the subject, standing near the end of the bench, raises a hand and asks if the same thing would work with a bigger plastic bowl from the sink. The teacher pauses, looks toward the sink, and says they can try something similar later if there is time, then moves on to repeat the demonstration for the students at the back table.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: air pressure holding a card against an inverted glass of water

episode.observableAction: On a mild morning in the shared courtyard, the subject kneels beside a small bicycle, slowly working a hand pump on the rear tire and checking the soft rubber with their thumb between strokes. After a few minutes, the subject sets the pump down, wipes their hands on their trousers, and walks over to the laundry lines to hang a damp T-shirt on a low wire, leaving the bicycle standing near the wall. While the subject clips the shirt with two clothespins and reaches for another item from the basket, the caregiver comes out carrying a grocery bag, notices the bicycle, and walks straight to it. Without calling to the subject, the caregiver picks up the pump, fits it to the valve, and quickly adds several firm strokes of air until the tire looks round and taut. The caregiver taps the tire with their fingers, nods once, leans the bicycle back against the wall, and sets the pump neatly beside it. When the subject turns back from the laundry line a moment later, the rear tire is already fully inflated and the caregiver is heading toward the courtyard gate with the grocery bag.

On an early evening in the shared courtyard, the subject stands near the laundry lines holding a nearly dry towel while the caregiver and younger sibling come out carrying a plastic bag of clothespins. The caregiver mentions that the subject once dropped a whole basket of wet clothes in a puddle "last winter" and tells the sibling not to overload the basket. The subject pauses, looks over, and says it was actually in the summer because they remember wearing shorts and sandals. The caregiver shakes their head and replies that it was cold and they were both wearing jackets, so it must have been winter. The subject insists again that it was warm and points toward the corner of the courtyard where the puddle had been, saying the sun was out and they were hanging T-shirts. The sibling, setting the bag down, chimes in that they remember watching from the window and seeing the subject in a big sweater. The subject frowns slightly, repeats that they were in shorts, and adds that the grandparent had opened the kitchen window because it was hot. The caregiver answers that the window was open to let steam out from cooking and that they clearly remember telling the subject to hurry because it was getting dark early. After a brief back-and-forth about whether it was dark early or still bright, the caregiver shrugs, says it does not matter when it was as long as they are more careful now, and starts clipping a sheet to the line while the subject silently turns back to hang the towel and the sibling begins handing up clothespins.

modelOutput.observableAction: In the shared courtyard near the laundry lines, the subject holds a nearly dry towel while the caregiver and younger sibling arrive with a plastic bag of clothespins, then they briefly argue about whether a past incident of dropping a basket of wet clothes in a puddle happened in winter or summer, each giving specific details like clothing, daylight, and an open kitchen window, before the caregiver ends the discussion by saying the timing does not matter and begins clipping a sheet while the subject hangs the towel and the sibling hands up clothespins.

episode.observableAction: In the practical science room on an autumn afternoon, the science teacher tells the class that heavier objects do not fall faster than lighter ones if air resistance is the same, holding up a thick textbook in one hand and a thin exercise notebook in the other. Several students murmur, and the teacher places both items side by side at the edge of a high lab bench. Standing near the front, the subject quickly pulls a metal ruler and a small eraser from their pencil case, steps closer to an empty section of bench, and says they want to try something. While the teacher pauses to watch, the subject holds the ruler and eraser level with each other over the tiled floor, counts "one, two, three" under their breath, and lets them go at the same time. The class watches as the ruler and eraser hit the floor almost together with two small clacks. The subject immediately picks them up, repeats the drop once more from the same height, then looks back toward the teacher, who nods and resumes explaining the point to the rest of the class.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: objects of different mass fall at the same rate in the absence of air resistance

episode.observableAction: In the practical science room on a late-morning lesson, the science teacher writes "Salt makes water boil faster" on the board and tells the class that many people repeat this but it is not exactly true. The teacher sets two identical metal beakers on adjacent gas burners, pours the same amount of tap water into each, and says that one will be left plain while salt will be added to the other. Standing at one of the front benches, the subject raises a hand and asks if they can help check it. When the teacher nods and steps aside, the subject comes forward, takes a plastic measuring spoon from the tray, and carefully measures a level spoonful of salt into a small dish the teacher holds out. At the teacher’s direction, the subject tips the salt into the second beaker, stirs it with a glass rod, then places a thermometer in each beaker and reads the starting temperatures aloud while a few classmates watch the clock on the wall. As the burners heat the beakers, the subject leans close to eye level with the water, calls out when the first small bubbles appear in each, and then announces the times when each beaker reaches a rolling boil, glancing between the clock and the thermometers. When both are boiling, the subject reports that the times are very close, and the teacher turns off the gas taps and tells the class to write down the numbers in their notebooks while the subject steps back to their seat.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: claim that adding salt makes water boil faster

modelOutput.observableAction: In the practical science room, the teacher writes "Salt makes water boil faster" on the board, sets up two identical beakers of water on gas burners, and invites the subject to help; the subject measures a spoonful of salt into one beaker, stirs it, places thermometers in both beakers, reads the starting temperatures aloud, watches for the first bubbles, calls out the times when each beaker reaches a rolling boil while checking the clock and thermometers, then reports that the boiling times are very close and returns to their seat as the teacher turns off the gas and tells the class to write down the numbers.

episode.observableAction: In a late-morning science class, the teacher stands at the front of an ordinary classroom and tells the students to copy a diagram from the board showing the Sun, Earth, and Moon, adding that the Moon is always visible at night and never in the daytime. Several students begin writing without comment. Sitting near the middle of the room, the subject stops copying, raises a hand, and says aloud that they have seen the Moon in the sky during the afternoon on the way home from school. A few classmates turn in their seats and one quietly laughs. The teacher pauses, looks at the subject, and replies that the Moon is a "night thing" and that the class should just write what is on the board. The subject keeps their hand up and adds that last week, during a football game at the river fields, they pointed out a pale Moon to a friend before sunset. More students look over; one student shakes their head and another mutters that it does not matter. The teacher sighs, says the textbook explains phases later and that they will "sort it out then," and tells everyone to get back to copying. The subject lowers their hand, opens their notebook again, and resumes drawing the diagram while the room settles and the teacher continues the lesson.

modelOutput.observableAction: In a late-morning science class, the teacher tells students to copy a Sun–Earth–Moon diagram while stating the Moon is only visible at night, the subject raises a hand twice to report seeing the Moon in the afternoon before sunset, some classmates react with laughter or dismissal, the teacher briefly responds that the Moon is a “night thing” and says the textbook will explain phases later, then instructs everyone to continue copying, and the subject lowers their hand and resumes drawing the diagram.

episode.observableAction: On an early evening at the neighborhood community workshop, the subject walks into the main hall where folding chairs face a makeshift stage and several large canvases lean against the side wall. Expecting more painted city scenes like ones they have seen there before, the subject stops short in front of a tall canvas that instead shows only a rough rectangle of flat grey paint with a single real tram ticket glued crookedly near one corner. The subject steps closer until they are within arm’s length, tilts their head, and slowly traces the air around the edges of the ticket, then along a faint pencil line that runs off the top of the canvas. After a moment, they glance back toward the doorway, look along the row of other canvases that include more recognizable bridges and streets, and then return to stand directly in front of the grey piece, shifting their weight from one foot to the other while continuing to look back and forth between the plain painted surface and the small, printed numbers on the ticket.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: grey canvas with glued tram ticket

episode.observableAction: In the late afternoon, the subject and their grandparent stand in the shared courtyard near the laundry lines, watching a light drizzle fall. The grandparent points toward the cloudy sky and tells the subject that when it rains, the clouds are "emptying out" and then they go away. The subject looks up at a thick bank of grey clouds that still covers most of the sky and says that the clouds are still there and asks how they can be empty if they are not gone yet. The grandparent pauses with a clothespin in hand, looks up as well, and repeats that the clouds are emptying, not empty yet, while clipping another wet shirt to the line. The subject continues to look between the clouds and the grandparent, asking why the rain sometimes stops but the same clouds stay over the buildings. The grandparent shrugs, says that the clouds move slowly and will go later, and then tells the subject to pass over the next piece of laundry from the basket. The subject hands up a small towel and glances back at the sky while the grandparent pins it beside the other clothes.

After school in the shared courtyard, the subject is looking at a tram route map they brought home for a project and tells the caregiver, “The driver said it takes twenty minutes from the loop to school, but the map says it’s only three stops. That’s not far.” The caregiver casually explains, “Three stops is always just a few minutes; it’s quick.” The subject frowns, points at the printed timetable on the map, and says, “But here it says 7 minutes and 7 minutes and 6 minutes, that’s already more than twenty.” The caregiver pauses, looks more closely, and corrects themselves: “You’re right, it adds up. I was thinking of when the tram doesn’t have to wait. Sometimes it stops longer, so it can be twenty minutes.” The subject nods slowly, still tracing the numbers with a finger, and repeats, “So three stops can be quick or long, it depends how long it waits.”

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: printed tram route map and timetable the subject brought home from school

episode.observableAction: On a dry mid-morning in the shared courtyard, the subject and their younger sibling are playing a game where they toss a small rubber ball against the wall and take turns catching it. After a few rounds, the sibling throws the ball, misses the catch, and runs to pick it up, but then immediately throws again without handing it over. The subject says, “Hey, you missed, now it’s my turn.” The sibling replies, “No, I get another go if I drop it.” The subject shakes their head and answers, “We said one throw each, even if you drop it.” The sibling insists, “But that’s not fair, I’m smaller.” The subject pauses, then says, “Okay, how about this: you get two throws, but if you drop both, then it’s my turn.” The sibling thinks for a moment, nods, and says, “Two throws for me, one for you.” The subject agrees, “Yeah, two for you, one for me,” and they restart the game using the new rule, counting out loud, “One… two… now my turn,” as they continue tossing the ball against the wall.

On a late afternoon at the community workshop, the subject walks in with their caregiver during a small neighborhood open day. Along one wall, children’s paintings are clipped to a string. The caregiver steers the subject toward the display and says, “Look, these are from the Saturday class.” The subject stops in front of a large sheet showing a dark blue river with thick, bright orange lines across the top. Leaning closer, the subject traces the air just above one of the orange strokes and says, “They painted the lights on the bridge like big stripes.” The caregiver glances at the label under the picture, reads the name and age aloud, and adds, “They must have done it at night by the river.” The subject keeps looking at the painting, shifts slightly to the side, and then points again at the orange lines, saying, “All the lights are going the same way.” After a few more seconds, the caregiver touches the subject’s shoulder and suggests, “Let’s see the other ones too,” and they move slowly along the row of pictures.

On a mild afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject wheels out the household’s only small bicycle, checks the tires by pressing them with their thumbs, and starts to climb on. The younger sibling comes through the doorway holding a plastic bag with two bread rolls and calls, “I need the bike, Grandma said hurry to the shop.” The subject, already with one foot on a pedal, replies, “I’m using it, I’m going to ride around.” The sibling steps closer, grabs the handlebar, and tugs it toward the gate, saying, “No, I have to go now, she’s waiting for the bread.” The front wheel twists sideways between them. The subject tightens their grip and says, “You can walk, I said I’d ride after homework.” The sibling shakes their head and answers, “It’s too far to walk, and she told me to take the bike.” For a few seconds they both hold the handlebars, the bike stuck between them. Then the subject lets out a short breath, lifts one hand off, and says, “Fine, you go, but bring it straight back.” The sibling immediately swings a leg over the frame, nods quickly, and pushes off toward the courtyard gate while the subject stands back, watching the sibling pedal out to the street.

modelOutput.observableAction: On a mild afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject wheels out the small bicycle, checks the tires with their thumbs, and starts to climb on when a younger sibling arrives holding a plastic bag with two bread rolls, says they need the bike because Grandma told them to hurry to the shop, grabs the handlebar and tugs it toward the gate as the subject insists they are using it and the sibling must walk, until after a brief struggle over the twisted front wheel the subject releases one hand, says the sibling can go but must bring it straight back, and then watches as the sibling mounts the bike and pedals out through the courtyard gate to the street.

episode.observableAction: During a morning gym class at the public school, the subject lines up with classmates along the painted baseline while the teacher explains a simple relay: each student is to run to a cone, pick up a small rubber ring, run back, and hand it to the next person. When the teacher blows the whistle, the first few students in each line sprint off. When it is the subject’s turn, they run quickly to the cone, but instead of grabbing one ring they scoop up the whole stack and jog back, clutching all of them against their chest. Several classmates start laughing and calling out, “Hey, you took them all!” and “We need those!” The subject slows, looks at the other lines now waiting empty-handed, and hesitates near their own team. The teacher steps forward, raises a hand to pause the noise, and says in a clear voice, “Only one ring each, remember.” The subject nods, turns around, and walks back toward the cone, dropping two rings on the floor before carefully setting the rest back on the marker. They then pick up a single ring, run it back to their line, and pass it to the next student as the relay resumes with a bit of lingering giggling from the others.

In the late afternoon light of the shared courtyard, the subject stands near the laundry lines while the caregiver shakes out a damp sheet and the younger sibling kicks a ball against the wall. The sibling suddenly says, “Remember when we got stuck on the tram and missed Grandma’s show?” The caregiver, pinning the sheet, replies, “We didn’t miss it, we were early and had to wait outside.” The subject looks over and says, “No, we were late. The tram stopped at the broken track and we had to walk from the other stop.” The caregiver pauses, frowns slightly, and answers, “That was another time. For Grandma’s show we got there before the doors opened.” The sibling stops the ball with a foot and insists, “It was the same day, I was holding the flowers and they got squashed on the tram.” The subject shakes their head and says, “The flowers got squashed when it rained and we ran from the loop, that was for her birthday, not the show.” The caregiver reaches for a clothespin and says, “I remember standing in the cold outside the hall with you two, and the doors were still shut. We weren’t late.” The sibling replies, “But the lights were already on inside when we came, I saw them through the glass.” The subject answers, “The lights were on because they were practicing, we were waiting on the steps.” The three of them stand there for a moment, the caregiver continuing to hang the sheet while the sibling nudges the ball in small circles and the subject leans against the low wall, and then the caregiver says, “Anyway, we got in before Grandma started playing,” and turns back to the laundry as the sibling resumes kicking the ball and the subject watches silently.

modelOutput.observableAction: In the late afternoon courtyard, the subject stands near laundry lines while the caregiver shakes out a damp sheet and the younger sibling kicks a ball, and the three briefly argue about whether they were early or late to Grandma’s show before the caregiver ends the exchange and returns to hanging the sheet as the sibling resumes kicking the ball and the subject watches in silence.

episode.observableAction: On a late afternoon at the community workshop, the subject stands in front of the small lending shelf where several thin paperbacks and magazines lean in two uneven rows. A handwritten sign above reads, “Take one, bring one back.” The subject runs a finger along the spines, pauses over a brightly colored sports magazine, then shifts it aside to look at the titles behind it. They pull out a stapled booklet with a plain cover that reads “Fixing Small Things at Home” and flip it open, glancing at a page with simple line drawings of a dripping tap and a loose bicycle chain. After a brief look back at the sports magazine and a comic book with a torn corner, the subject closes the repair booklet, tucks it under one arm, and walks over to the sign-in notebook on the nearby table. They pick up a pen, write their name and the booklet’s title on the next blank line, and then leave the shelf area with the booklet still under their arm as another person steps in to browse the remaining items.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: "Fixing Small Things at Home" repair booklet

episode.observableAction: On a gray mid-afternoon at the public school, the subject walks down the corridor toward the practical science room carrying an exercise book and a clear plastic folder with loose worksheets. A printed notice on the door reads, “After-school help: Wednesdays 16:15–17:00.” The subject glances at the clock above the stairwell showing 16:30, then pushes the door handle. Inside, the lights are off and the benches are empty except for a few stacked stools near the back. The subject steps in, looks around, and calls the teacher’s name once in a normal voice. There is no reply. They walk to the front bench where a small pile of marked test papers sits under a paperweight, flip through the top few pages, then set them back in place. After a moment, the subject goes to the open doorway, leans out to look up and down the corridor, and sees no staff nearby. They return to the room, place their exercise book on a front bench, and sit down, opening it to a page of half-finished problems. After a few minutes of working quietly, the subject looks up when footsteps approach; the same teacher from gym class appears in the doorway carrying a stack of folders, pauses, and says, “Oh, I’m just locking up this room; the science teacher’s not here today.” The subject closes the exercise book, nods, and stands. The gym teacher gestures toward the corridor and adds, “You’ll have to catch them tomorrow,” before switching on the lights briefly to check the windows, then turning them off again. The subject tucks the exercise book and worksheets back into the plastic folder, walks past the teacher into the corridor, and heads toward the stairwell as the teacher locks the science room door behind them.

modelOutput.observableAction: On a gray mid-afternoon at the public school, the subject walks down the corridor toward the practical science room carrying an exercise book and a clear plastic folder, finds the room dark and empty, briefly calls the teacher’s name, looks through a small pile of marked test papers on the front bench, then sits to work quietly in the exercise book until a gym teacher arrives, explains the science teacher is absent and the room is being locked, after which the subject gathers their materials, leaves into the corridor, and walks toward the stairwell as the teacher locks the door.

episode.observableAction: On a late Sunday morning in a side room of the community workshop, a small group of adults sit on folding chairs in a loose circle while the subject and their grandparent share a chair near the doorway. A middle-aged man at the front finishes reading a short passage aloud from a thin booklet resting on his knee: “Each person is responsible for their own intention, and no one can carry the burden of another.” He lowers the booklet and asks if anyone wants to comment. The grandparent leans slightly toward the subject and quietly repeats, “No one can carry the burden of another,” tapping the booklet cover with one finger. The subject looks at the booklet, then at a handwritten poster on the wall where the same sentence is copied in larger letters. After a brief pause, the subject shifts forward, resting their forearms on their knees, and continues to look between the man holding the booklet and the poster as another attendee begins to speak about the line. When the man passes the booklet around the circle, the grandparent takes it, opens to the marked page, and holds it so the subject can see the printed sentence before handing it on to the next person.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: short booklet discussing personal responsibility for one’s own intention

episode.observableAction: On a warm mid-afternoon in the school gym, a small group of students, including the subject, stand along one side wall while a teacher sets up a portable microphone and a pair of old speakers for an informal talent segment at the end of a sports day. When the teacher calls the subject’s name, a few classmates clap and whistle as the subject walks to the center of the marked basketball court holding a folded sheet of paper. The teacher hands over the microphone, steps back toward the wall, and nods. The subject unfolds the paper with one hand, raises the microphone, and begins to recite a short poem they have written. After the first few lines, a loud squeal of feedback bursts from the speakers, and the microphone cuts out with a pop. Several students laugh and a couple of voices call, “We can’t hear you!” The subject lowers the microphone, glances toward the teacher, and stands still while the teacher crosses the floor, takes the microphone, and taps it. Nothing comes through the speakers. The teacher bends to check the cable at the small amplifier, flicks a switch, and then straightens up, saying in an ordinary voice to the subject, “You can keep going without it if you want, or we can stop here.” The subject looks at the loose semicircle of students sitting on the floor, then steps a little closer to them, folds the paper in half, and starts the poem again in a raised voice without the microphone. The gym quiets enough that the words carry; a few students at the back lean forward to listen. The subject reaches the end of the poem, lowers the paper, and there is a brief mix of clapping and scattered chatter as they walk back to the side wall while the teacher coils the dead microphone cable and waves the next volunteer forward.

modelOutput.observableAction: In the school gym during a warm mid-afternoon, a small group of students, including the subject, stand along one wall while a teacher sets up a portable microphone and old speakers for an informal talent segment at the end of sports day; when the teacher calls the subject’s name, some classmates clap and whistle as the subject walks to the center of the basketball court holding a folded sheet of paper, takes the microphone, unfolds the paper, and begins reciting a short poem until loud feedback squeals from the speakers and the microphone cuts out, prompting laughter and shouts of “We can’t hear you!” from a few students, after which the subject waits while the teacher tests the silent microphone, checks the amplifier, and then tells the subject they can continue without it or stop, and the subject moves closer to the loose semicircle of seated students, raises their voice to restart the poem without amplification, finishes it as the gym quiets enough for the words to carry, and then returns to the side wall amid brief clapping and scattered chatter while the teacher coils the dead microphone cable and signals the next volunteer.

episode.observableAction: Late on a cool Saturday morning, the subject stands near the laundry lines in the shared courtyard, bouncing a scuffed rubber ball against the wall. A slightly older child from another flat, carrying a plastic bag with chalk pieces and a small toy car, comes through the courtyard door. After watching a couple of bounces, the other child walks over, sets the bag down, and says they are going to draw a road and parking spaces with chalk on the concrete and asks the subject if they want to play cars together. The peer points to a clear patch of ground near the bicycle rack and holds up the toy car, waiting. The subject stops bouncing the ball and looks from the ball to the chalk bag and the empty concrete where the road could be drawn.

On a bright weekday morning, the caregiver comes out into the shared courtyard carrying a plastic laundry basket and a small bag of clothespins, with the subject and younger sibling trailing behind. After setting the basket down near an empty section of line, the caregiver clips one corner of a wet sheet to the wire, then turns to the subject and asks them to hand up clothespins one by one so the sheet does not drag on the ground. The caregiver holds the sheet taut with one hand and reaches out the other. The subject stands by the basket, picks a pin from the bag, and places it into the caregiver’s open palm each time they ask, while the younger sibling watches from a few steps away, occasionally nudging a loose pin along the concrete with their foot. As the last corner is fastened and the sheet hangs clear of the ground, the caregiver nods toward the basket and asks the subject to push it a little farther down the line for the next load, and the subject shoves it along the path until it bumps gently against the post.

On a mild afternoon, the subject sits on the low step by the courtyard wall with a stub of blue chalk, adding short lines to a rough track they have been drawing on the concrete. A cardboard box lid lies open beside them, with a few small stones and a plastic bottle cap arranged like tiny buildings. The older peer from another flat comes through the courtyard carrying a ball, slows when they reach the drawing, and crouches down. They set the ball aside, lean over the chalk lines, and point to a curved section where the subject has drawn a narrow bridge over a scribbled "river." The peer says that the bridge looks too skinny for cars and taps the space next to it, suggesting they could make another lane or add a tunnel under the river. As the subject looks at the spot the peer is indicating, the caregiver steps out of the stairwell door with a mesh bag of clothespins, pauses, and glances down at the chalk layout. The caregiver comments that the little stones lined up by the edge look like a row of shops along the road, then continues toward the laundry lines, leaving the subject and peer by the drawing.

On a breezy afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject kneels near a clear patch of concrete, rolling their familiar scuffed rubber ball back and forth to mark out the corners of an imaginary goal in front of the wall. A few chalk lines from older drawings are still faintly visible nearby. The younger sibling comes out of the stairwell door holding a small plastic bucket and, spotting the ball, walks straight over and picks it up. The subject reaches for the ball and says they are using it to play a shooting game against the wall. The sibling hugs the ball to their chest and says they want to take it over to the laundry lines to play a pretend "shop" by dropping it into the bucket. The subject tugs lightly at the ball with both hands while the sibling pulls back the other way, turning their shoulders away from the wall toward the laundry area. For a few seconds they stand close together, each gripping part of the ball and insisting on their own game, until the ball slips from their hands, bounces once between them, and rolls a short distance toward the bicycle rack.

On a cool Saturday morning in the school gym, a mixed group of students lines up along the painted sideline for a simple relay game during a community sports session. The teacher in charge explains that each person must run to a cone at the far end, circle it, and come back to tag the next runner’s hand. The subject stands third in their line, with the familiar older peer from their building a few places behind them. When the teacher blows a whistle, the first runners in each line sprint out and back, slapping the next person’s palm. As the second runner in the subject’s line returns, the subject steps forward, but instead of holding out their hand they turn and start running as soon as the other student is a few steps away. The second runner has to chase and tap the subject’s shoulder from behind, and the subject hesitates and glances back, briefly slowing the lane. The teacher blows the whistle twice in quick bursts and calls out that the subject started early and needs to come back to the line and wait for a proper hand tag. Several students in nearby lines look over. The subject jogs back to the sideline cone, stands beside the second runner, and this time holds out their hand. When the teacher nods, the second runner slaps the subject’s palm and the subject sets off again toward the far cone while the older peer in the same line watches and shifts forward a step.

episode.observableAction: On a chilly early evening at the community workshop, the subject stands near the back wall of the hall where folding chairs have been pushed aside for a small performance. The subject, who had been standing near a bulletin board expecting a more conventional song, stays where they are, watching the performer move past them and then back toward the front as the tram voices and violin sounds continue to blend and cut off abruptly.

episode.observableAction: On a late Saturday morning in the school gym during an open three-on-three basketball scrimmage, the subject stands near the top of the key while a small group of students and the same teacher from earlier sports events watch from the sideline. With the score tied and the next basket deciding which team stays on the court, a teammate passes the ball to the subject, who is unguarded. The subject takes a quick dribble and goes up for a layup, but the ball hits the underside of the rim and drops straight down out of bounds. A few players on both teams groan and one laughs briefly, and the teacher blows the whistle, calling that possession goes to the other team. As the teams jog back on defense, the older peer from the subject’s side claps the subject once on the shoulder and tells them to get back and guard the wing. The subject turns, runs to a spot near the sideline, and raises their arms to defend as play resumes with the inbound pass.

On a gray Saturday late afternoon at the community workshop, the subject arrives carrying a school notebook and a plastic folder, walks past the bulletin board, and stops in front of the main hall door where a handwritten notice is taped at eye level. The paper reads that the usual weekend study help session with the familiar teacher is canceled for the day due to illness and will resume the following week. The subject stands still for a moment reading the note, then looks through the small window in the hall door at the empty room with its stacked chairs and darkened projector. After a brief pause, they turn away from the door, walk over to an unoccupied side table near the lending shelf, set down their notebook and folder, pull out a worksheet and a pen, and sit alone at the table, opening the notebook and beginning to write on the worksheet without any staff or teacher present nearby.

On a warm Saturday afternoon in the school gym during an open community basketball run, the subject joins a mixed-age scrimmage organized by the familiar teacher, who keeps score from the sideline with a clipboard. Midway through a game to eleven points, with several students and a few younger kids watching from the bleachers, the subject’s team runs a fast break after a steal. The older peer dribbles up the court, points toward the basket, and passes the ball ahead to the subject cutting down the middle. The subject catches the pass in stride, takes two steps, and goes up alone for a layup, but the ball slips off their fingers, hits the front of the rim, and bounces straight back, missing the basket completely. A couple of players on both teams call out in surprise, one on the subject’s team groans loudly and slaps their own forehead, and a younger kid on the sideline laughs and imitates the missed shot with an exaggerated arm motion. The ball is rebounded by an opponent, who quickly dribbles out toward the wing. The teacher blows the whistle once, calls out the updated score in a neutral voice, and signals for play to continue. The subject lands, looks briefly toward the sideline where the miss drew reactions, then turns and sprints back on defense. episodes.observableAction: In the practical science room at school on a winter afternoon, the class gathers around a lab bench while the teacher fills a clear glass with tap water and slowly slides a stiff piece of white card over the top. Holding the card in place with one hand, the teacher flips the glass upside down over a tray and then carefully removes the supporting hand so the card stays pressed against the mouth of the glass and the water does not spill. Several students murmur, and the teacher explains that the air underneath is pushing up on the card. When the teacher sets the glass back upright and tips the water into the tray, the subject, standing near the end of the bench, raises a hand and asks if the same thing would work with a bigger plastic bowl from the sink. The teacher pauses, looks toward the sink, and says they can try something similar later if there is time, then moves on to repeat the demonstration for the students at the back table.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: air pressure holding a card against an inverted glass of water

episodes.observableAction: On a mild morning in the shared courtyard, the subject kneels beside a small bicycle, slowly working a hand pump on the rear tire and checking the soft rubber with their thumb between strokes. After a few minutes, the subject sets the pump down, wipes their hands on their trousers, and walks over to the laundry lines to hang a damp T-shirt on a low wire, leaving the bicycle standing near the wall. While the subject clips the shirt with two clothespins and reaches for another item from the basket, the caregiver comes out carrying a grocery bag, notices the bicycle, and walks straight to it. Without calling to the subject, the caregiver picks up the pump, fits it to the valve, and quickly adds several firm strokes of air until the tire looks round and taut. The caregiver taps the tire with their fingers, nods once, leans the bicycle back against the wall, and sets the pump neatly beside it. When the subject turns back from the laundry line a moment later, the rear tire is already fully inflated and the caregiver is heading toward the courtyard gate with the grocery bag.

In the shared courtyard near the laundry lines, the subject holds a nearly dry towel while the caregiver and younger sibling arrive with a plastic bag of clothespins, then they briefly argue about whether a past incident of dropping a basket of wet clothes in a puddle happened in winter or summer, each giving specific details like clothing, daylight, and an open kitchen window, before the caregiver ends the discussion by saying the timing does not matter and begins clipping a sheet while the subject hangs the towel and the sibling hands up clothespins.

In the practical science room on an autumn afternoon, the science teacher tells the class that heavier objects do not fall faster than lighter ones if air resistance is the same, holding up a thick textbook in one hand and a thin exercise notebook in the other. Several students murmur, and the teacher places both items side by side at the edge of a high lab bench. Standing near the front, the subject quickly pulls a metal ruler and a small eraser from their pencil case, steps closer to an empty section of bench, and says they want to try something. While the teacher pauses to watch, the subject holds the ruler and eraser level with each other over the tiled floor, counts "one, two, three" under their breath, and lets them go at the same time. The class watches as the ruler and eraser hit the floor almost together with two small clacks. The subject immediately picks them up, repeats the drop once more from the same height, then looks back toward the teacher, who nods and resumes explaining the point to the rest of the class.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: objects of different mass fall at the same rate in the absence of air resistance

episodes.observableAction: In the practical science room, the teacher writes "Salt makes water boil faster" on the board, sets up two identical beakers of water on gas burners, and invites the subject to help; the subject measures a spoonful of salt into one beaker, stirs it, places thermometers in both beakers, reads the starting temperatures aloud, watches for the first bubbles, calls out the times when each beaker reaches a rolling boil while checking the clock and thermometers, then reports that the boiling times are very close and returns to their seat as the teacher turns off the gas and tells the class to write down the numbers.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: claim that adding salt makes water boil faster

episodes.observableAction: In a late-morning science class, the teacher tells students to copy a Sun–Earth–Moon diagram while stating the Moon is only visible at night, the subject raises a hand twice to report seeing the Moon in the afternoon before sunset, some classmates react with laughter or dismissal, the teacher briefly responds that the Moon is a “night thing” and says the textbook will explain phases later, then instructs everyone to continue copying, and the subject lowers their hand and resumes drawing the diagram.

On an early evening at the neighborhood community workshop, the subject walks into the main hall where folding chairs face a makeshift stage and several large canvases lean against the side wall. episodes.observableAction: On a dry mid-morning in the shared courtyard, the subject and their younger sibling are playing a game where they toss a small rubber ball against the wall and take turns catching it. After a few rounds, the sibling throws the ball, misses the catch, and runs to pick it up, but then immediately throws again without handing it over. When the teacher blows the whistle, the first few students in each line sprint off. When it is the subject’s turn, they run quickly to the cone, but instead of grabbing one ring they scoop up the whole stack and jog back, clutching all of them against their chest. Several classmates start laughing and calling out, “Hey, you took them all!” and “We need those!” The subject slows, looks at the other lines now waiting empty-handed, and hesitates near their own team. The teacher steps forward, raises a hand to pause the noise, and says in a clear voice, “Only one ring each, remember.” The subject nods, turns around, and walks back toward the cone, dropping two rings on the floor before carefully setting the rest back on the marker. They then pick up a single ring, run it back to their line, and pass it to the next student as the relay resumes with a bit of lingering giggling from the others.

In the late afternoon courtyard, the subject stands near laundry lines while the caregiver shakes out a damp sheet and the younger sibling kicks a ball, and the three briefly argue about whether they were early or late to Grandma’s show before the caregiver ends the exchange and returns to hanging the sheet as the sibling resumes kicking the ball and the subject watches in silence.

On a late afternoon at the community workshop, the subject stands in front of the small lending shelf where several thin paperbacks and magazines lean in two uneven rows. A handwritten sign above reads, “Take one, bring one back.” The subject runs a finger along the spines, pauses over a brightly colored sports magazine, then shifts it aside to look at the titles behind it. They pull out a stapled booklet with a plain cover that reads “Fixing Small Things at Home” and flip it open, glancing at a page with simple line drawings of a dripping tap and a loose bicycle chain. After a brief look back at the sports magazine and a comic book with a torn corner, the subject closes the repair booklet, tucks it under one arm, and walks over to the sign-in notebook on the nearby table. They pick up a pen, write their name and the booklet’s title on the next blank line, and then leave the shelf area with the booklet still under their arm as another person steps in to browse the remaining items.

A middle-aged man at the front finishes reading a short passage aloud from a thin booklet resting on his knee: “Each person is responsible for their own intention, and no one can carry the burden of another.” He lowers the booklet and asks if anyone wants to comment. The grandparent leans slightly toward the subject and quietly repeats, “No one can carry the burden of another,” tapping the booklet cover with one finger. The subject looks at the booklet, then at a handwritten poster on the wall where the same sentence is copied in larger letters. After a brief pause, the subject shifts forward, resting their forearms on their knees, and continues to look between the man holding the booklet and the poster as another attendee begins to speak about the line. When the man passes the booklet around the circle, the grandparent takes it, opens to the marked page, and holds it so the subject can see the printed sentence before handing it on to the next person.

On a mild afternoon, the subject sits on the low step by the courtyard wall with a stub of blue chalk, adding short lines to a rough track they have been drawing on the concrete. A cardboard box lid lies open beside them, with a few small stones and a plastic bottle cap arranged like tiny buildings. The older peer from another flat comes through the courtyard carrying a ball, slows when they reach the drawing, and crouches down. They set the ball aside, lean over the chalk lines, and point to a curved section where the subject has drawn a narrow bridge over a scribbled "river." The peer says that the bridge looks too skinny for cars and taps the space next to it, suggesting they could make another lane or add a tunnel under the river. As the subject looks at the spot the peer is indicating, the caregiver steps out of the stairwell door with a mesh bag of clothespins, pauses, and glances down at the chalk layout. The caregiver comments that the little stones lined up by the edge look like a row of shops along the road, then continues toward the laundry lines, leaving the subject and peer by the drawing.

On a breezy afternoon in the shared courtyard, the subject kneels near a clear patch of concrete, rolling their familiar scuffed rubber ball back and forth to mark out the corners of an imaginary goal in front of the wall. A few chalk lines from older drawings are still faintly visible nearby. The younger sibling comes out of the stairwell door holding a small plastic bucket and, spotting the ball, walks straight over and picks it up. The subject reaches for the ball and says they are using it to play a shooting game against the wall. The sibling hugs the ball to their chest and says they want to take it over to the laundry lines to play a pretend "shop" by dropping it into the bucket. The subject tugs lightly at the ball with both hands while the sibling pulls back the other way, turning their shoulders away from the wall toward the laundry area. For a few seconds they stand close together, each gripping part of the ball and insisting on their own game, until the ball slips from their hands, bounces once between them, and rolls a short distance toward the bicycle rack.

In a school gym during a community sports relay, students line up while a teacher explains they must run to a far cone, circle it, and return to tag the next runner’s hand; when the whistle blows and the second runner in the subject’s line comes back, the subject starts running early without a hand tag, is called back by the teacher for starting before being properly tagged, then returns to the sideline, offers their hand, receives the palm slap, and runs again toward the far cone as an older peer in the same line watches.
The subject enters the community workshop, examines several books on a small lending shelf, selects a comic-style magazine, and carries it to a nearby table with a sign-out notebook and pen.

episodes.observableAction: On a chilly early evening at the community workshop, the subject stands near the back wall of the hall as a young local performer sets a portable speaker on a chair, presses a button, and begins a piece that mixes recorded tram announcements, door chimes, and snippets of overlapping conversations with slow, drawn-out violin notes, walking in a slow circle around the room, sometimes turning their back to the listeners, once stopping beside the subject to hold a long, wavering note while a loud recorded braking sound plays, and briefly pointing the violin toward the ceiling while the announcements play on without violin before moving back toward the front as the tram voices and violin sounds continue to blend and cut off abruptly.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: experimental performance mixing tram sounds with live violin

episodes.observableAction: On a late Saturday morning in the school gym during an open three-on-three basketball scrimmage, the subject stands near the top of the key while a small group of students and the same teacher from earlier sports events watch from the sideline. With the score tied and the next basket deciding which team stays on the court, a teammate passes the ball to the subject, who is unguarded. The subject takes a quick dribble and goes up for a layup, but the ball hits the underside of the rim and drops straight down out of bounds. A few players on both teams groan and one laughs briefly, and the teacher blows the whistle, calling that possession goes to the other team. As the teams jog back on defense, the older peer from the subject’s side claps the subject once on the shoulder and tells them to get back and guard the wing. The subject turns, runs to a spot near the sideline, and raises their arms to defend as play resumes with the inbound pass.

On a gray Saturday late afternoon at the community workshop, the subject arrives carrying a school notebook and a plastic folder, walks past the bulletin board, and stops in front of the main hall door where a handwritten notice is taped at eye level. The paper reads that the usual weekend study help session with the familiar teacher is canceled for the day due to illness and will resume the following week. The subject stands still for a moment reading the note, then looks through the small window in the hall door at the empty room with its stacked chairs and darkened projector. After a brief pause, they turn away from the door, walk over to an unoccupied side table near the lending shelf, set down their notebook and folder, pull out a worksheet and a pen, and sit alone at the table, opening the notebook and beginning to write on the worksheet without any staff or teacher present nearby.

During a community basketball scrimmage in the school gym, the subject joins a fast break, receives a pass on a cut to the basket, misses an uncontested layup that draws audible reactions and mimicry from players and a younger spectator, then quickly turns to sprint back on defense, acknowledges a brief pat and instruction from an older teammate near midcourt, and moves to guard the ball handler with arms raised as play continues.
